Home Care for Bedridden Patients: How to Prevent Pressure Ulcers

Bedridden patients need careful, regular care to reduce the risk of pressure ulcers and support comfort, safety and overall well-being. This guide covers repositioning, daily skin checks, hygiene, moisture control, nutrition, pressure-relieving devices and when to seek professional medical support.

Why Home Care for Bedridden Patients Matters

Bedridden patients need regular and careful care. When a person stays in the same position for a long time and cannot move independently, certain parts of the body are exposed to constant pressure. This can reduce blood flow to the skin and underlying tissues, increasing the risk of pressure ulcers.

Pressure ulcers are more common in older adults, patients after stroke, people recovering from major surgery, patients with paralysis, limited mobility, diabetes, poor circulation or general weakness. These skin injuries can cause pain, increase the risk of infection and slow down recovery.

Proper home care helps reduce the risk of pressure ulcers and supports the patient’s comfort, safety and overall well-being.

What Are Pressure Ulcers?

Pressure ulcers, also known as bedsores or pressure injuries, are areas of skin and tissue damage caused by prolonged pressure. They usually develop over bony areas of the body.

Common areas include:

  • lower back and tailbone
  • hips
  • heels
  • elbows
  • shoulder blades
  • back of the head
  • knees and ankles

Early signs may include redness, skin color changes, pain, warmth, burning, swelling or firmness in one area. If these signs are ignored, the skin may break down and turn into an open wound.

Who Is at Higher Risk?

The risk of pressure ulcers is higher in people who cannot change position by themselves. The risk also increases when the patient has poor nutrition, dehydration, urinary or bowel incontinence, fragile skin, reduced sensation or poor blood circulation.

Patients with diabetes, advanced age, paralysis, severe weakness or long hospital stays need especially careful skin monitoring and prevention.

Caring for a bedridden patient is not limited to giving food and medicine. It also includes regular repositioning, skin checks, hygiene, moisture control and monitoring the patient’s general condition.

Regular Repositioning

One of the most important steps in preventing pressure ulcers is regular repositioning. A patient should not remain in the same position for too long.

If the patient is in bed, their position should be changed regularly. For example, they may be positioned on the back, left side and right side in rotation. Avoid dragging or pulling the patient across the bed, as this can damage the skin through friction and shear.

If the patient sits in a chair or wheelchair, pressure on the same area should also be reduced. Special cushions, position changes and short rest periods in bed may help, depending on the patient’s condition.

Daily Skin Checks

The patient’s skin should be checked every day. Pay special attention to the tailbone, heels, elbows, shoulder blades, hips, back of the head and skin folds.

Warning signs include:

  • redness
  • skin discoloration
  • swelling
  • pain
  • burning or warmth
  • firmness
  • blisters
  • cracks
  • wet areas or open wounds

If redness does not disappear after pressure is removed, it may be an early sign of a pressure injury. In this case, pressure on that area should be avoided and a healthcare professional should be contacted.

Skin Hygiene and Moisture Control

The skin should be kept clean and dry. Prolonged moisture weakens the skin and increases the risk of breakdown.

If the patient has urinary or bowel incontinence, diapers, pads and bedding should be changed on time. The skin should be cleaned gently and dried carefully by patting, not rubbing.

If the skin is dry, a suitable moisturizer may be used after advice from a healthcare professional. Do not apply creams, oils, alcohol-based products or ointments to irritated skin or open wounds without medical guidance.

Pressure-Relieving Mattresses, Cushions and Supports

Special pressure-relieving mattresses, cushions and positioning supports may help reduce pressure on vulnerable areas. These devices help distribute body weight more evenly.

Soft pillows may also be used to support the legs, arms, back or side position. For example, placing a pillow between the knees can reduce pressure and friction when the patient lies on the side.

However, support devices must be used correctly. A poorly placed pillow may increase pressure instead of reducing it. For patients at high risk, a care plan should be discussed with a doctor or nurse.

Nutrition and Hydration

Nutrition plays an important role in skin health and tissue repair. The body needs enough protein, vitamins, minerals and fluids to maintain healthy skin and support healing.

If the patient eats poorly, loses weight, drinks too little, has swallowing problems or refuses meals, medical advice is needed. Some patients may require an individual nutrition plan.

Pressure ulcer prevention is not only about external skin care. It is also connected to the patient’s overall health, circulation, nutrition and mobility.

Safe Moving and Turning

When turning, sitting up or moving a bedridden patient, care must be taken to avoid friction and injury. Do not drag the patient across the bed.

Use a draw sheet, moving aids or help from another person when needed. Movements should be slow and coordinated. It is also helpful to explain each step to the patient before moving them.

Safe movement protects the patient’s skin and also reduces the risk of back, shoulder or arm injuries for the caregiver.

When Should You Contact a Healthcare Professional?

Contact a healthcare professional if the patient has persistent redness, an open wound, fluid discharge, pus, unpleasant odor, swelling, strong pain or fever.

Important: Trying to treat pressure ulcers at home without professional guidance can be risky. The wrong dressing, unsuitable ointment or improper wound cleaning can increase infection risk.

A healthcare professional can assess the skin or wound, recommend the right dressing, create a care plan and decide what treatment or follow-up is needed.

Conclusion

Preventing pressure ulcers is one of the most important parts of home care for bedridden patients. Regular repositioning, daily skin checks, good hygiene, moisture control, proper nutrition, pressure-relieving devices and timely professional help can reduce risks and prevent complications.
